parts.title: Part 1
parts.context: A father phones a holiday sports camp to enrol his son for a week in the summer.
script: Good morning, Kingfisher Sports Camp, Megan speaking.
Oh, hello. I'm ringing to enrol my son for the summer holiday camp. I picked up one of your leaflets at the library.
Lovely. I can take all the details now over the phone, which is quicker than the website. Could I have your son's surname first, please?
Is that Brennen, with an E in the middle?
Brennan, thank you. And how old is he? We take children from seven to twelve.
Well, he'll be ten in October, but he's nine at the moment, so I suppose it's nine.
Nine is perfect, he'll be in the middle group. Now, could I take your postcode, please?
NR3 7GH. Thanks. Now, which week would you like? We run the camp for six weeks. The first one starts on 7 July, and then every Monday after that.
Well, we're away at the start of the month, so we were hoping for the week beginning the 14th.
Ah, let me look. I'm afraid that week is full, and there's a waiting list as well. The following week, starting on the 21st, still has places, though.
That should be fine. Yes, put him down for the 21st.
Great. Now, every child tries a bit of everything during the week, but they also choose one main activity. The choices are football, tennis, swimming or climbing.
He's football mad, but he plays that at school all the time. Actually, he's been asking to try the climbing wall ever since his birthday, so let's go for that.

Climbing it is. I should warn you that the climbing groups are small, so it's a good idea to book early, which you've done. Now, the camp normally finishes at 4 o'clock, but the climbing group finishes half an hour earlier because they have to hand back all the safety equipment.
So you'd like me to collect him at 3.30.
That's right, 3.30 for the climbers. Parents are welcome to wait in the cafe.
Perfect, I finish work at 3 anyway. How much will it be?
The normal price is 95 pounds a week. But if you book before the end of this month, there's an early booking price of 85 pounds.
Today's the 18th, so that's still all right. 85 it is. Do I pay now?
No, we'll send you an invoice by email, and you have two weeks to pay. Now I need to ask about health. Does he have any allergies we should know about?
Yes, he's allergic to peanuts. Not nuts in general, just peanuts. He used to react to eggs as well, but he grew out of that years ago. He's got an inhaler for his asthma, too, but he rarely needs it.
Thank you, I'll make a note of the peanuts, and the staff will keep his inhaler in the first aid room. Now, we also need an emergency contact number. Could I have yours?
I'm usually at work, and I can't always answer. It would be better to ring my wife. Her mobile is 07839 405 126.
No, it ends 126. One, two, six.

Sorry, 07839 405 126. Got it. Is there anything else I should tell you? Yes, a few things about what to bring. He'll need trainers, a packed lunch, and a hat and sun cream. We provide towels for the swimming, so he doesn't need one of those.
And the thing everybody forgets is a water bottle with his name on it. It gets very hot in the sports hall and we can't give out cups.
A water bottle, with his name on. I'll write that down. Is there anything to sign?
I'll email you a consent form with the invoice. Just sign it and bring it on the first morning.
Wonderful. Thank you very much for your help, Megan.
You're welcome. We'll look forward to seeing Oliver on the 21st. Goodbye.

parts.title: Part 2
parts.context: A farm manager gives an induction talk to seasonal workers on their first morning at a fruit farm.
script: Good morning, everyone, and welcome to Pennington Orchards. Grab a seat wherever you can, and there's tea at the back if you haven't had one yet. My name's Greg Halloran, and I'm the farm manager. Over the next fifteen minutes I'm going to tell you how the day works, what you need to know about pay and clothing, and where everything is on the farm.

Let's start with the working day. Last year we began at 7, but the afternoons were so hot that the fruit was soft by the time it reached the packing shed, so now we start earlier. Breakfast is served in the canteen from 5.30, and I'd strongly recommend that you eat something, because you won't have another break for three hours. But picking itself starts at 6 o'clock sharp. That means being in the field by 6, not walking out of the canteen at 6. The supervisors will be counting heads, and anyone who arrives late loses the first half hour's pay.

We have two breaks. There's a tea break at 9 and lunch is at half past 12. Now, a word about mobile phones. I know you all want to ring home and send photographs, and that's fine. But you must not use your phone in the rows, not even to check the time. We've had fruit dropped, and one person walked straight into a ladder while looking at a screen. So phones are for your breaks only. You can use them in the canteen or outside, wherever you like, but not while you're working.

Now, pay. Everybody asks about this, so let me be clear. During your first week, you're paid by the hour, whatever you pick. That gives you time to learn without worrying about speed. After that, the raspberry and strawberry pickers move on to a rate per kilo. The plum pickers stay on the hourly rate for the whole season, because the work on the ladders is much slower.

Clothing. We give you gloves and a sun hat, and they're yours to keep. We also provide waterproof jackets, which you'll collect from the store. What we can't provide is boots. The fields are very muddy after rain, and you need your own pair, so if you haven't got any, the farm shop in town sells them quite cheaply. Please don't turn up in trainers tomorrow, because I'll have to send you back.

What if you're ill? It happens, and nobody will be angry. But please telephone your supervisor, Maria, before the shift starts. Don't ask a friend to pass on a message, and don't send a text, because we may not see it in time. If you're away for more than two days, we'll need a note from a doctor.

Now let's talk about the farm itself, so you know where you'll be working. If you look at the map on the wall, you'll see the farm is quite spread out. The big plastic tunnels in the north are called the polytunnels, and that's where our strawberries grow. Most of you will start there, because the plants are low and the work is gentler on the back. Behind them, you'll see the lower orchard, which is where we grow our plums. The plum pickers work from ladders, and we'll give you a short training session on the ladders before you start.

Once the fruit is picked, it goes straight to the packing shed, the long building next to the car park. Teams in there weigh the fruit, check it and put the labels on. It's quite skilled work, so you'll only be moved in there after a couple of weeks. Then, from the packing shed, the boxes go to the cold store at the end of the track. That's where all the fruit is kept overnight until the lorries collect it at dawn.

Finally, the yard behind the barn. This is where the empty crates come back from the fields. They need to be cleaned and stacked ready for the next day. It's not glamorous, but it's an important job, and everyone helps out there once a week. You may see some people working near the pipes in the lower field. They're maintaining the irrigation system, and that's done only by our permanent staff, so please keep away.

Any questions? No? Then let's get you into your groups. Your supervisors will give you your name badges, and then we'll walk to the fields together. Thank you again, and I hope the sun stays out for us.

parts.title: Part 3
parts.context: A student, Chloe, discusses her field trip report on river pollution with her tutor, Dr Hughes.
script: Come in, Chloe. Take a seat. I've had a look at your draft report on the river, so shall we go through it?
Yes, please. I'm a bit nervous, to be honest. I don't know whether I've done enough.
Well, first of all, remind me why you picked the River Aldwin. I think I suggested the Marsh Brook at the start.

You did, and I did look at it, but it only runs through fields. The Aldwin goes through farmland first and then through the town, so I could compare samples from both areas. It isn't the nearest river to the campus, though. The brook is actually closer, and I had to catch two buses to reach my first site.
That's a sensible reason, and you should say so in the introduction. Did you have any problems during the fieldwork?

A couple. I'd planned four sampling sites, but the fourth one was on private land, and the owner wouldn't let me in. So I had to move the site to the footbridge about two hundred metres away. My testing kit was fine, I checked it against the lab equipment twice, and the weather stayed dry, so that wasn't a problem.
Good. Now, your results. You wrote that you expected the highest nitrate levels in the town, near the old industrial estate.
I did, but it turned out differently. The highest reading was actually at the second site, just below the farm drain. In the town, the levels were lower than I'd predicted.
That is interesting, and it's worth more discussion. But I do have one concern. You collected all your samples on a single day.
Yes, the third of May. I ran out of time to go back.

I understand, but it means your sample is quite small. One day's data can't tell you what's normal for the river. So you can't make firm claims. Use words like suggests and may indicate, rather than proves. If you do that, the report will be perfectly acceptable.
Okay, I'll change the wording. Could I go through the sections with you, one by one? I want to make sure I fix the right things.

Of course. Start with the introduction. It's nearly four pages, which is far too long for a report of this size. There's lots of background about pollution in general that you don't need. I'd cut it by half.
Right. I wasn't sure what to leave out.

Keep only what leads to your question. Now, the methods section. You've described the sites well, there's plenty of detail there. But it's hard for a reader to picture where they are. A simple map with the four sites marked would help enormously.
I've got one from the survey website. I could mark the sites on that.

That would be fine, as long as you say where it came from. Next, the results. At the moment, all your figures are in the paragraphs, and it's quite hard to read. Put the numbers in a table, and then you only need to describe the main pattern in the text.

A graph might work too, but with only four sites, a table is clearer. Then the discussion. This is where you should connect your results to what other people have found. You read some good studies on farm runoff in the first term, and none of them appears here.
Oh, I didn't think I'd be allowed to use them.

Of course you can. That's what makes a discussion strong. Finally, the conclusion. The content is good, but you've written it in the present tense, as if you were still in the field. It should all be in the past tense. It's a small thing, but it will matter.
I see. So that's the introduction, the map, the table, the earlier studies and the tense. I'll write that down.
That's all, really. You've done a good job. When do you plan to hand it in?
The deadline is the twelfth. I was thinking of going to the writing workshop at the study centre before then.
I don't think you need to. If you send me the new draft by Friday, I'll look at it over the weekend, and then you'll have time for the last changes.
That's very kind. All right, I'll email it to you on Friday morning.
Excellent. And don't worry so much. You've got good data, so just be careful in the way you describe it.
Thank you, Dr Hughes. That's really helpful. I feel much better now.

parts.title: Part 4
parts.context: A lecturer gives a talk on desert plants and the ways in which they survive.
script: Good afternoon, everyone. Today I'd like to talk about desert plants, and in particular the remarkable ways in which they survive in some of the harshest conditions on Earth. When most people think of a desert, they imagine an empty landscape of sand. In fact, deserts are home to thousands of species of plants, and many of them are found nowhere else.

First, what do we mean by a desert? The usual definition is a place that receives less than 250 millimetres of rain in a year. That is about a quarter of the rainfall of a typical European city. But the number doesn't tell the whole story. In many deserts the rain doesn't fall evenly. A year's rain can arrive in a single storm, followed by months, even years, of drought. So plants have to cope with long dry periods, intense heat, and often very poor soil.

Botanists usually divide desert plants into three main groups, according to the strategy they use. The first group I'll call the escapers. These plants don't really fight the drought. They simply avoid it. They survive the dry years as seeds, and when it finally rains, they germinate, grow, flower and produce new seeds, all in a very short time. Some of these annuals can complete their entire life cycle in six weeks. If you're lucky enough to visit a desert after rain, you'll see the ground covered with wildflowers, and a few weeks later it's all gone again.

What's fascinating is how these seeds know when to germinate. If they sprouted after a light shower, the seedlings would die when the soil dried out. So the seeds contain a chemical inhibitor that prevents germination. The only way to remove it is for a lot of water to wash through the soil. Experiments suggest that around 15 millimetres of rain is needed, which is just enough to give the seedling a chance. So in effect, the seed measures the rainfall.

The second group are the succulents, and the best known are the cacti. Succulents store water in their stems or leaves, and they use it very slowly. Their roots are shallow, usually only a few centimetres below the surface, but they spread out very widely, so that they can catch even a short shower before the water evaporates. The giant saguaro cactus is a good example. It has deep ribs that fold like an accordion. When it rains, the ribs expand, and the plant can swell by hundreds of litres within a few hours. Then, as it uses the water, it slowly shrinks again. A large saguaro can hold enough water for a full year.

The third group is very different. These plants don't store water at all. They reach for it. Their roots go down very deep, to the water table below. The mesquite tree is a famous example. In older books you'll often read that its roots reach 50 metres. That figure was a mistake, which has been repeated for decades. When engineers dug beside a mesquite tree in a mine, they measured roots of around 30 metres, which is still extraordinary.

Now, whichever strategy they follow, most desert plants lose as little water as possible through their leaves. Some have tiny leaves, or none at all, and the leaves may be replaced by spines. Others cover their leaves with a thick waxy coating that seals in the moisture. Many have fine, pale hairs on the surface, and these reflect sunlight, which keeps the leaf cooler. And then there's the way plants breathe. Plants take in carbon dioxide through tiny openings called stomata, but each time the stomata open, water escapes. Many desert plants have solved this problem by opening them only at night, when it's cool, and storing the carbon dioxide until the sun rises. This special kind of photosynthesis is found in cacti and in many other desert species.

Why does all this matter? Well, as the climate changes, many regions of the world are becoming drier, and farmers are struggling with their crops. Scientists are now studying the genes of desert plants, to find out how they cope with so little water. The long-term aim is to develop crops that are better able to tolerate drought. Some people are also trying to conserve desert seeds in seed banks, in case the habitats they come from disappear.

So, to sum up, desert plants are far from helpless. They escape, they store, or they reach, and they have many clever ways of cutting down their water losses. Next week we'll move on to look at how animals survive in the same conditions. Thank you, and please do read the chapter before then.

passages.title: Mobile phone plans compared
paras: A  Nimbus Basic. A simple SIM-only plan for people who use their phones lightly. It costs 9 pounds a month on a 12-month contract and includes 5 GB of data with unlimited calls and texts. Customers who pay by direct debit receive a reduction of 1 pound each month. No handset is included, so you will need to keep your existing phone. This plan is available to customers over the age of 18.

B  Nimbus Plus. Designed for customers who want a new phone without a large payment at the start. For 14 pounds a month on a 24-month contract, you receive a mid-range handset at no extra cost, together with 30 GB of data and unlimited calls and texts. Insurance against accidental damage to the handset is also included, although customers must pay the first 25 pounds of any claim.

C  Kestrel Flex. A plan for people whose needs change from month to month. The contract lasts 12 months, but each month you can choose 5 GB, 15 GB or 30 GB through the Kestrel app, and the price changes to match, from 10 pounds to 16 pounds. Unused data is not carried over to the following month. Calls and texts are unlimited.

D  Kestrel Max. The company's premium plan, at 25 pounds a month on a 24-month contract. There is no limit on the amount of data you may use, and 100 minutes of calls to numbers abroad are included each month. New customers also receive six months of a video streaming service free of charge. A handset can be added for an extra 10 pounds a month.

E  Harbour Go. The cheapest plan of the five, at 6 pounds a month for 2 GB of data and 300 minutes of calls. There is no contract: the plan runs for 30 days at a time, and customers can cancel at any time by sending a text message. It is popular with students, who sometimes keep it as a second line for travelling.

passages.title: Notice to residents: planned interruption to water supply, Marsh Lane area
paras: Hartwell Water will be replacing an ageing water main under Beacon Road on Tuesday 12 March. As a result, the supply to homes and businesses on Beacon Road, Marsh Lane, Tanner's Row and Ivy Close will be switched off between 9.00 am and 3.00 pm. Our engineers will do all they can to restore the supply on time, but residents are advised to store some water in advance.

Free bottled water will be available from Hartwell Library in Church Street between 8.30 am and 6.00 pm on the day. Residents who rely on water for medical treatment, such as home dialysis, should telephone our Customer Care Line on 0800 555 0142 by Friday 8 March, so that we can arrange an alternative supply for them.

When the supply returns, the water may look cloudy or slightly brown for a short time. This is harmless, but we advise you to run your cold tap for 5 minutes, or until the water runs clear, before you drink it. Please do not use washing machines or dishwashers until the water has cleared, as discoloured water may stain clothes.

Because the work is planned and the interruption is brief, customers are not entitled to compensation and bills will not be reduced. We apologise for the inconvenience and thank residents for their patience.

passages.title: Using the pool car: guidance for staff
paras: The company owns one pool car, a white electric hatchback, for staff who need to visit clients or attend meetings away from the office. It is kept in bay 14 of the rear car park and is available to all permanent employees who have a full driving licence.

Booking. The car must be booked through the booking calendar on the intranet at least 24 hours before you need it. The maximum booking is two consecutive days. If you need the car for longer, you must obtain written approval from your line manager and send it to the Facilities team. Bookings cannot be made by telephone or by email.

Who may drive. You must be at least 23 years old and have held a full licence for at least two years. The Human Resources department checks every driver's licence once a year, and you will be asked to show it. If you receive penalty points on your licence, you must tell your line manager at once.

Collecting and returning the car. Keys are kept at reception, and you may collect them at any time between 8.00 am and 5.30 pm. Before you leave the car park, walk round the vehicle and report any damage to Facilities. Please write the mileage at the start and end of your journey in the logbook kept in the glove compartment, together with the reason for the trip. Keys must be returned to reception by the end of the same working day.

Charging. The charging cable is stored in the boot. The car must be returned with the battery at least 40 per cent charged, so that it is ready for the next driver. Charging points are available at the front of the building, and the cost of any charging done away from the office will be repaid through the expenses system if you keep the receipt.

Accidents. If you are involved in an accident, however small, report it to the police if anyone is injured, and then to Facilities as soon as possible. You must complete an incident report within one working day. Smoking and eating are not permitted in the car, and only company employees may travel as passengers.

passages.title: Making the most of workplace mentoring
paras: Workplace mentoring is a partnership between two employees: a mentee, who wants to develop, and a mentor, who has more experience and is willing to share it. A mentor is not the same as a line manager. A line manager checks that your work is done well and on time. A mentor, in contrast, is there to listen, to ask questions and to help you think about your career. For this reason, mentors are always chosen from a different department from their mentee, so that the relationship can stay informal and free from pressure.

The company's scheme lasts for 12 months. It is open to any employee who has successfully completed their probation period, which normally lasts six months. Mentors are volunteers, and they are asked to attend a half-day training course, held twice a year, before they are matched with a mentee. The course explains how to listen actively and how to give feedback in a helpful way.

Mentors and mentees should meet for about one hour every month, either in person or by video call. The first meeting is the most important, because this is when you agree your goals for the year. Many people find it useful to write these down, and to look at them again every three months. It is the mentee's responsibility to prepare for each meeting, which means bringing topics to discuss. If the mentee comes without any ideas, the meeting can become a general chat, and that does not help anyone.

Confidentiality is essential. Whatever you discuss with your mentor must stay private, and your mentor should not report on it to your manager. The only exception is when something you say suggests that you or someone else may be in danger. In that case, your mentor must pass the information to the Human Resources department. Both people should understand this from the beginning.

At the end of the 12 months, mentor and mentee meet with a member of the Human Resources team to review what has been achieved. They may decide to end the arrangement, or to continue it informally. Mentees who would benefit from a different point of view are encouraged to ask for a new mentor for the following year. Last year, 7 out of 10 mentees said that the scheme had made them feel more confident at work.

passages.title: On two wheels through the traffic: how the bicycle courier business grew
paras: A  In the early 1980s, anyone who stood on the pavement of a busy city centre at midday might have noticed a new kind of worker. Slipping between the buses and taxis went young men and women on bicycles, with large bags slung across their backs and radios clipped to their shoulders. They were couriers, and what they carried was almost always paper. Contracts, legal papers, architects' drawings and bank documents all had to be delivered across the city within the hour, and the roads were so congested that a van could take longer to travel three kilometres than a cyclist took to cover five. For a few busy years, there was no faster way to send an important document across a crowded city centre. The work was fast, badly paid at first and often dangerous, but it attracted a loyal following of people who loved the freedom of the streets.

B  Messenger boys on bicycles were not new. A century earlier, young riders had carried telegrams and notes through the streets, until the telephone made most of them unnecessary. The modern courier business owes its beginning to a handful of individuals who saw that old idea could work again. One of them was Rob Haldane, who in 1983 started a company called Quickspoke in the northern city of Calderport. Haldane had been a messenger himself while a student, and he had noticed that solicitors and bankers were willing to pay well for a signed original to arrive within an hour. He began with three riders and a second-hand radio, and he did the dispatching from his kitchen table.

C  Quickspoke grew quickly, as did dozens of similar firms in other cities. The key to the system was the radio. A dispatcher, sitting at a desk, took telephone orders from clients and then called out jobs to the nearest rider, who confirmed by radio and set off. A good dispatcher could keep thirty riders working at the same time. Most riders were self-employed and were paid for each delivery, rather than receiving a weekly wage, so a fast rider could earn more than a messenger in an office. The job gained a certain glamour. Riders developed their own slang, their own clothes and their own social lives, and the courier became a familiar character in films and music.

D  The golden age did not last. In the 1990s, fax machines, and then email, began to replace paper in business. A contract that once had to be carried across town could now be sent in seconds. Within a decade the number of riders in many cities fell by about half, and many of the larger companies closed. Haldane's firm survived, but only because he cut its prices and reduced its fleet. The mobile phone replaced the radio, although for most firms it served only as a more convenient way of calling riders.

E  What saved the industry was online shopping. By the 2010s, people were ordering goods on their phones and expecting them the same day, and restaurants began to deliver meals. Couriers turned out to be a good fit for this new demand. Companies built smartphone apps that showed customers exactly where their parcel was, and riders found that they could handle more jobs than before. Some businesses found other uses for their skills. In Calderport, Quickspoke began to carry laboratory samples between hospitals, a job that needed speed and reliability, and it now has a contract with the regional health service. Supermarkets and clothing retailers have followed, and a rider who once carried a single envelope may now deliver a dozen small parcels on a single round.

F  The new work was not without problems. Most delivery riders in the app era are still self-employed, and critics argue that they have few of the protections that other workers enjoy, such as sick pay or holiday pay. There have been disputes in several countries over whether these riders should be classed as employees. Safety is another concern, as riders are often working to tight deadlines in heavy traffic. A few companies have responded by guaranteeing a minimum payment for each hour worked, and by providing helmets and insurance, but the debate is far from settled.

G  The latest development is the cargo bike, a sturdy, three-wheeled or two-wheeled machine, often with an electric motor, that can carry loads of up to 200 kilograms. Cities that want to reduce traffic and pollution have begun to encourage them, and some now charge vans to enter the centre. A trial run by a council in the Midlands found that on routes shorter than three kilometres, cargo bikes were on average faster than vans, and cheaper to run. Haldane, now in his seventies, is no longer on the road, but he still visits the Quickspoke depot twice a week. He says he is not surprised: forty years ago, he reminds anyone who will listen, the idea was exactly the same. Whether the courier of the future rides a bicycle, a cargo bike or something not yet invented, the central idea of speed through crowded streets seems certain to survive.
